National Rostering Service

Replacing a 20-year-old tool that cost more to patch every year. I led design on a rostering service for more than 8,000 on-road staff, shaped with the people who use it.

Context

National Highways keeps traffic officers on the road across the country, around the clock. Someone has to decide who works where and on which shift — early, late or variable — and then keep re-deciding it as people go sick, take leave and swap shifts.

Every shift has a threshold: the number of people it needs to run safely. When a shift falls below it, officers are on the road without enough cover. Rostering isn’t admin. Getting it wrong is dangerous.

The problem

The resource management tool was 20 years old and had become unmanageable. It was a third-party web app held together by ‘sticky plaster’ patches, and every patch cost more than the last. The infrastructure was old and slow, and the people using it every day had learned to work around it.

When we spoke to roster managers, they told us they had to keep seven tabs open, on average, just to use the system — before counting email or anything else they needed. Every one of them was working on a device with 8GB of memory at most. Many had to stop work and wait for their machine to catch up.

A lot of them blamed their laptops for not being powerful enough. In reality, the system was poorly optimised. And each change or ‘optimisation’ made it worse: performance dropped and costs only went up. It reached a boiling point, where managing a roster was difficult, slow and too expensive to maintain.

‘The current system takes too many clicks.’

That sounds like a small complaint. It isn’t. When a routine change takes a manager through several screens, and there are thousands of changes a month, the cost shows up in staff time, in overtime, and in gaps nobody caught. The goals were to bring running costs down, make rosters simpler to manage, and give staff a tool they were happy to use.

Research

We started with the people doing the work. I ran workshops with users across the country, at every level of seniority, from the officers on the road to the managers building their rosters. We also shadowed roster managers, interviewed staff, read through support tickets and reviewed the system’s architecture.

For the interviews, we started from what we needed to understand and turned each into an open question.

Workshops across the country

From pain points to requirements

  1. Users shared what got in their way
  2. Together, we prioritised those pain points
  3. They workshopped solutions to the biggest ones
  4. Then prioritised the solutions too
  5. Which became the service’s requirements

What we heard

Five pain points

  • A cluttered interface
  • Manual data entry
  • Limited view of the schedule
  • Rigid rules
  • Poor links to HR systems

And one request, again and againShow me what a week looks like at a glance.

Asking users to prioritise their own problems, and then their own solutions, meant the requirements came from the people who’d live with the result, not from the old system’s feature list.

Designing with stakeholders

There was no separate testing phase. Instead, the design was shaped in the open, through close collaboration with stakeholders: a workshop with more than 20 of them, and regular sessions where we put wireframes and prototypes in front of the people who knew rostering best and changed them together.

I restructured the information architecture around how often people do things, mapped the service in a blueprint, and split the manager and staff views so each group only sees what they act on. From there, we moved from low-fidelity wireframes to medium-fidelity prototypes, and the design went through three big shifts.

  1. Searchable availabilityFind who’s free for a shift, without leaving the rota.
  2. Context menusRight-click a shift to swap, cover or extend it, where the manager is already looking.
  3. A colour-coded team viewEvery shift type has its own colour, so a manager can read a week at a glance.

Reading a week at a glance

The request we heard most was to see a week at a glance. So every day on the rota carries a short code: how many lates, earlies and variable shifts it has.

1L.3E.0V 1Late3Early0Variable

On its own, that’s a count. Set against each shift’s threshold, it becomes demand analysis: green when a day has the cover it needs, red when it doesn’t. A gap stops being something a manager has to go looking for. It finds them.

Journeys

The most important journey is the one that keeps people safe: spotting a shift that’s below threshold and filling it with someone who can legally work it.

Fill shift

Recommend, don’t just list

Staff are ranked by availability, rest between shifts and hours this period, with the reason shown next to each name. The best match is at the top.

Working-time check

Catch it before it’s saved

If an assignment would break a working-time rule, the manager sees why at the moment they choose, with the rest gap laid out on a timeline.

Around it sit the screens that keep a manager ahead of the next gap: an activity feed for sickness, swaps and leave, each showing what it does to the threshold; a staff profile with someone’s recent shift pattern at a glance; and insights on where and why shifts are going short.

The design

The interface is calm on purpose. Most of a rota is fine, so most of the screen is quiet: white space, navy for structure, and soft colours for the three shift types. Colour is saved for what needs attention. Red means a shift is below its safe threshold, and nothing else is red.

The same components work on a deep navy background. The shift colours stay the same, and the status colours become darker tints so a full grid stays readable without glaring.

The design system

Every screen is built from one small system: colour tokens for brand, shift types and status (with a navy set), and components built in auto layout — shift cards, threshold cells, banners, activity items, insight cards and the controls around them. Each kind of news has one tone, so a manager learns the colours once.

Handover

When the design phase finished, we ran a full handover to the development agency chosen to build it. We didn’t hand it over and walk away: we’ve stayed in the build, giving design assurance so the finished product keeps the experience we designed.

What we handed over

Everything needed to build it right

  • Documentation of every design decision and the reason behind it
  • Interactive prototypes with annotated user flows
  • Component specifications and design system guidelines
  • The research findings, so the build team had the context behind each decision

How we stay involved

Design assurance through the build

  • Regular design reviews with the development team
  • Answering design questions and clarifying as needed
  • Checking what’s built against the design specifications
  • Joining sprint reviews to bring a UX perspective

Working this way keeps the design intact through development, while leaving room for practical changes when technical constraints call for them.

It also lasted beyond the screens. Collaboration across teams improved, stakeholders were aligned on what was being built and why, and a new feedback repository gave users a standing way to be heard. The project became an internal case study for user-centred design.

Projected results

Based on our prototyping and the efficiencies already gained in the design process, we projected these outcomes once the system is in place:

Several departments across the organisation have already asked to adopt the system once it launches, a strong sign of confidence in what it will deliver.

Future proofing

As the service evolves, we set up key measures to track, test and improve it over time.

Support tickets

Fewer tickets is a sign users trust the data the system gives them. We track volume, category and time to resolve, and the data points us at the areas that need the most work.

Quarterly targets for reduction

Task completion time

Research showed the old journeys were convoluted and frustrating. We monitor how long key tasks take, through automated tracking and periodic sessions with users.

65%less time to create a roster, in early data

System performance

The new service sits within the tools people already use, and simpler journeys mean far fewer tabs open at once, the thing that used to strain people’s devices. We track CPU use on users’ machines.

40%less resource use than the legacy system, in early measurements

These measures guide the development roadmap, so the system keeps meeting users’ needs while delivering savings for the organisation.

Lessons learned

The project reinforced a few principles for designing enterprise services:

  • Understand the whole ecosystemRostering doesn’t exist in isolation. It’s connected to many other systems and processes.
  • Balance automation with controlAutomation saves time, but people still need to feel in control of critical decisions.
  • Design for different skill levelsThe system had to work for experienced roster managers and occasional users alike.
  • Prioritise performanceWith this much data, speed was central to whether people were happy using it.
  • Involve users throughoutWorkshops with users across the country surfaced problems and opportunities we wouldn’t have found on our own.

The service keeps evolving with user feedback and the organisation’s needs, which is why it was designed to flex.

What I’d do differently

We didn’t test the service with users before handover. The design came out of workshops and close work with stakeholders, which got us a long way, but stakeholders aren’t the same as the managers and officers using it at six in the morning.

Next time I’d put the prototype in front of frontline users early, and keep doing it. Managers build the roster, but the people living with it notice different problems.
